beats.say: When people worry about where computer chips come from, they look here. At Taiwan.
One industry study found about ninety percent of the world's most advanced chip-making capacity on this one island.
But turn the globe almost thirteen thousand kilometres, to a small town in the mountains of North Carolina.
This is Spruce Pine. About two thousand two hundred people live here.
On the hills around it, two companies dig up a white rock that the chip industry has found very hard to replace.
In September twenty twenty-four, a hurricane buried these mountains in rain. Both companies stopped work.
Chip sales last year came to nearly eight hundred billion dollars.
So why does all of that lean on one small town? And what happened when the town went dark?
To answer that, forget the chip for a moment. We need to talk about a bowl.
A chip starts as rock. Ordinary quartz rock is turned into silicon, and the silicon is cleaned until it is almost perfectly pure. Then comes the hard part.
A chip needs its silicon as one single crystal. Every atom in line, like tiles on a floor, and not one out of place.

The trick for growing one goes back to a Polish chemist, Jan Czochralski. The story goes that one evening he dipped his pen into molten tin instead of ink. When he lifted it, a thin thread of metal came up with it: a single crystal. He published the method in nineteen eighteen.
Chip makers still use his idea. They fill a bowl with chunks of pure silicon, and heat it past fourteen hundred degrees Celsius, until it melts.
They lower a tiny seed crystal until it just touches the surface.
Then they pull it up, very slowly, turning it as it rises. The liquid silicon freezes onto the seed, layer by layer, and a crystal grows.
The finished crystal is called an ingot. One quartz producer says a full ingot can weigh over five hundred kilograms and measure more than four metres.
The ingot is sliced into thin discs called wafers, each about a millimetre thick.
And chips are built on the wafers. The same company says one ingot can become about two million chips.
Now look again at the bowl.
It is called a crucible, and it has a terrible job. It must hold liquid silicon for days, without melting, cracking, or leaking anything into it.
Because the hot silicon slowly eats at the wall of the bowl. Whatever is in the wall ends up in the crystal. And a few stray atoms are enough to spoil the chips.
So the bowl must take the heat, and be almost as pure as the silicon itself. The answer is quartz: melted, and shaped into a milky white bowl.
And not just any quartz. In the top grade, fewer than ten parts in every million are anything else.
And a bowl does not last. That producer says one crucible pulls about eight ingots, over four hundred hours. So the world needs new bowls, all the time.
So here is the first surprise. The famous quartz is not in your phone. It is the bowl your phone's chips were born in.
Ordinary quartz is good enough to make the silicon. But quartz pure enough for the bowl is found in only a few places on Earth.
The best known of them is here, in the Blue Ridge mountains, around Spruce Pine.
The story the miners tell begins about three hundred and eighty million years ago, when two continents pushed together, and these mountains rose.
Deep underneath, molten rock was trapped. One company says it cooled slowly. The other says there was very little water around to carry impurities in.
Whichever it was, the result is a pale rock, holding quartz of rare purity.
The United States Geological Survey puts it at more than ninety-nine point nine nine nine percent pure.
China has announced large reserves of its own. In the first tests, the survey notes, their purity came in just below Spruce Pine's.
Two companies produce this quartz here. Sibelco, which sells it under the name Iota. And The Quartz Corp.
The Geological Survey counts no other producers in the whole country. And for most uses, it says, there is no economic substitute.
You will often hear that seventy to ninety percent of the world's supply comes from this one town. We went looking for where that number comes from.
We could not find it in any official record. The survey says world production figures are simply not available. It only estimates that the United States leads.
Here are numbers that are official. All the silicon wafers sold last year earned about eleven billion dollars. The chips built on them, nearly eight hundred billion.

And the pure quartz? Take the survey's estimate of tonnes sold, at its very top price, and America's whole supply is worth, at most, a little over one billion dollars a year. A speck, holding up a giant.
A speck can be fragile. In November two thousand eight, a fire broke out at one of the plants here. Investigators found no foul play. But it was a warning.
On the night of the twenty-sixth of September, twenty twenty-four, Hurricane Helene came ashore in Florida as a category four storm, and drove north.
In Spruce Pine, both quartz companies had already stopped work that day, before the worst arrived.
Then the rain came. Gauges just outside the town measured about twenty-four inches. That is sixty centimetres of water.
Rivers in the county rose to the highest levels ever recorded. Roads and bridges washed out. The power failed.
In this one county: more than two hundred landslides. About a hundred thousand trees down. And one person drowned in the river that runs through the valley.
And the railway that follows the river north, through a narrow gorge into Tennessee, was torn apart.
Far away, the people who make chips had one question. Was the quartz gone?
A week later, Sibelco reported its first look at the plants. They had, in its words, only sustained minor damage.
The Quartz Corp said its damage was mostly around side units. Later it said up to a quarter of its workers were out helping the town recover.
About two weeks after the storm, Sibelco said production and shipments had restarted. By late October, The Quartz Corp said its plants were gradually restarting too.
And there were stockpiles. The Quartz Corp pointed to safety stocks along the chain. Two big wafer makers did not even mention the storm in their next results.
So the mines had survived. What broke was everything around them.
About sixty miles of that railway were badly damaged. In the gorge, the track had to be built again, mile by mile.
Here the popular story goes wrong. Spruce Pine was not cut off from trains for a year. The railway says limited service near the town was back by the middle of January.
But the gorge took far longer. The whole line returned to service on the twenty-fifth of September, twenty twenty-five. Almost exactly one year.
The railway's own filings put the cost at about five hundred and twenty million dollars.
A year after the storm, trains ran the whole line again.
So was the world lucky? Partly. The storm stopped the quartz for weeks, not for years.
But look at what one small place needed before the bowls could flow again. Power. Roads and a railway. Clean water. And the people who live there.
Governments had seen part of this coming. A White House review in twenty twenty-one warned that the crucibles themselves came from a single source, or from abroad.
The industry's answer, so far, has not been to leave. Sibelco had already announced two hundred million dollars to double its capacity here, and a second expansion of around five hundred million.
Others are trying to catch up. A Chinese producer is building a plant for sixty thousand tonnes a year. Some bowl makers now line the inside with man-made silica.
And new chip factories keep rising, far from these mountains. India has approved twelve semiconductor units, including a fab at Dholera, in Gujarat.
Every one of them will need wafers. And India's solar makers, the government says, still rely substantially on imported wafers. Behind a great many of those wafers stands a quartz bowl.
We tend to picture a chokepoint as a narrow sea, watched by warships.
This one is a green valley, a pale rock, and about two thousand people.
The most advanced machines on Earth begin in a bowl. And the bowl begins here, in Spruce Pine.
